title: A TCP/IP Tutorial
summary: A tutorial on the TCP/IP protocol suite, focused on the steps in forwarding an IP datagram from source host to destination host through a router. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Follow a letter as it goes from your house through a post office to a faraway house, and see what each helper does.

questions: how is an ip datagram forwarded through a router
what is the tcp ip protocol stack
what is the difference between tcp and udp
subtitle: The layers and routing of internet protocol networks

tldr.problem: Networks need a common way to move data between computers across different types of physical networks. Each network has its own rules and addresses.
tldr.mechanism: TCP/IP provides a layered stack where IP creates a single logical network across physical networks, ARP translates addresses, and TCP or UDP handle traffic from applications.
tldr.outcome: The Internet works by stacking these protocols on top of each other. Routers forward packets by checking the IP address and consulting a routing table.

today: RFC 1180 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It remains a widely-used tutorial for understanding TCP/IP basics, though it does not describe the current state of the Internet at scale.

sections.title: What This Tutorial Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1180 is a guide to understanding TCP/IP, the set of protocols that power the Internet. It focuses on how an IP datagram travels from one computer to another, often passing through routers to cross network boundaries. The tutorial does not try to be complete; instead, it covers the minimum a network administrator or systems programmer needs to know. It uses examples from UNIX but explains concepts that apply to all TCP/IP implementations.

The tutorial moves from simple concepts (what is a datagram?) to more complex ones (how does a router decide where to send a packet?). Each section answers a specific question that network professionals face in their work.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide written for people who work with the Internet. It explains the basic ideas you need to know, using real examples from real networks.

sections.title: The Layered Stack
sections.content:
TCP/IP works as a series of layers, each sitting on top of the other. Applications like FTP or email sit at the top. Below them are TCP or UDP, which handle communication. Below that is IP, which manages routing. At the bottom are Ethernet drivers and the physical network. Each layer adds its own header to the data as it goes down, and strips its header off as data comes back up.

Data at different levels has different names: application messages, TCP segments or UDP datagrams, IP packets, and Ethernet frames. The structure does not change whether the computer is on one network or several. If a computer has multiple network connections, IP acts as a switch, routing data from one network interface to another. Routers are computers dedicated to this forwarding task.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a wedding cake with frosting layers. Your message starts at the top. Each layer wraps it in a new layer of frosting (a header). At the bottom, the package is ready to send on the cable.

sections.title: Addresses and the ARP Protocol
sections.content:
Every computer on Ethernet has a 6-byte Ethernet address (like 08-00-39-00-2F-C3), and every computer on an IP network has a 4-byte IP address (like 223.1.2.1). When IP needs to send a packet out onto the Ethernet, it must know the Ethernet address of the destination. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) translates IP addresses to Ethernet addresses using a table stored in memory.

When an ARP table entry is missing, the computer broadcasts an ARP request to all devices on the Ethernet. The device with the matching IP address sends back its Ethernet address, which gets stored in the table. From then on, the translation is instant. If no computer claims the address, the system discards the outgoing packet.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP address is like a street address; an Ethernet address is like a person's name. ARP is a directory that looks up the name when you know the address.

sections.title: Routing and the Route Table
sections.content:
The IP module is central to TCP/IP because it makes routing decisions using an in-memory table called the route table. When a packet arrives at a computer, IP checks whether the destination IP address is its own. If so, it passes the packet up to the application layer. If not, it checks the route table to decide whether to forward the packet and which network interface to use.

For computers on the same network, routing is simple: send directly to the destination. For computers on different networks, the packet must go through a router. The route table stores the IP network number as the key, a flag saying whether the destination is direct or indirect, the IP address of the router to use (if indirect), and the interface number. Network administrators manually configure this table, which is why mistakes in routing tables can break communication in hard-to-diagnose ways.
sections.plainLanguage: A routing table is like a mailbox with slots for different neighborhoods. When mail arrives, you check the address and drop it in the slot for that neighborhood.

sections.title: TCP and UDP: Two Ways to Send Data
sections.content:
UDP and TCP are the two main protocols that applications use to send data over IP. UDP is simple: it adds a port number (to identify which application gets the data), a length field, and a checksum, then sends it as a single datagram. Applications using UDP must handle losses and retransmission themselves. The advantage is speed; the disadvantage is unreliability.

TCP is more complex and guarantees that data arrives in order and without loss. It uses a sliding-window scheme with acknowledgments and timeouts. TCP applications can ignore network details and focus on their logic. TCP costs more CPU and bandwidth than UDP. The choice between them depends on the application: file transfers and login sessions use TCP; network monitoring and file serving often use UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP is like tossing a postcard in the mail: fast but you cannot promise it arrives. TCP is like a registered letter: slower but you get a receipt.

sections.title: What You Can Do with TCP/IP
sections.content:
The RFC lists several important applications. TELNET provides remote login over TCP; it has been around since the beginning of internet technology and is widely interoperable. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) also uses TCP and lets you copy files between computers. The r* commands (rsh, rcp, rwho) offer remote UNIX capabilities. NFS (Network File System) lets you mount remote file systems as if they were local disks. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) collects network statistics using UDP.

The set of applications grew beyond those listed in the RFC as the Internet expanded. Each application chooses TCP or UDP based on its needs, and new applications continue to be added without changing TCP/IP itself.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP/IP lets you do many things: log into a remote computer (TELNET), copy files (FTP), share files (NFS), and check network health (SNMP).
